evals.prompt: We have an existing Python FastAPI web application that streams Server-Sent Events (SSE) from an LLM for up to 90 seconds per request. Which serverless compute and ingress pattern should we choose?
evals.expected_output: Activates the serverless-architecture-and-cost-advisor skill, recommends wrapping the FastAPI app (`PORT=8080`) with **Lambda Web Adapter** and exposing it via a **Lambda Function URL** configured with `InvokeMode: RESPONSE_STREAM` (supporting up to 15 minutes duration and 20 MB streaming payloads at $0 extra API Gateway charge, optionally fronted by CloudFront OAC + AWS WAF).
expectations: Activates the serverless-architecture-and-cost-advisor skill and recommends the Lambda Web Adapter (`PORT=8080`) so FastAPI runs without rewriting routes into raw Lambda handlers
Explains why API Gateway's 29-second default integration timeout blocks 90-second SSE streams and recommends a Lambda Function URL with `RESPONSE_STREAM` (supporting up to 15 minutes and 20 MB)
Notes that Lambda Function URLs have $0 per-request API Gateway surcharge and can be secured with CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) and AWS WAF

evals.prompt: We run a steady-state, 24/7 JSON transformation service in ap-south-1 handling a flat 1,500 RPS (3.94 billion requests/month), where each request takes 100ms (80ms network I/O wait, 20ms CPU) at 1,769 MB (1 vCPU). Compare the architecture and monthly TCO break-even math across: (1) Standard Lambda On-Demand (`arm64`), (2) Lambda Managed Instances (LMI with `PerExecutionEnvironmentMaxConcurrency` and EC2 Compute Savings Plans), and (3) Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate (`arm64` Spot/Savings Plans). Include operational and thread-safety trade-offs.
evals.expected_output: Activates the serverless-architecture-and-cost-advisor skill, computes the Standard Lambda On-Demand cost for 3.94B requests (`~$788` in request charges + `3.94B * 0.1s * 1.7275 GB * $0.0000133334` = `~$9,076` duration = `~$9,864/mo`), explains how **Lambda Managed Instances (LMI)** eliminates per-invocation cold starts and packs multiple concurrent I/O-waiting requests (`PerExecutionEnvironmentMaxConcurrency` / `AWS_LAMBDA_MAX_CONCURRENCY`) onto customer-selected EC2 instance types covered by EC2 Compute Savings Plans / RIs (noting the 15–20 min capacity provider scale-out time and mandatory thread-safe `/tmp` isolation), and compares **ECS Fargate** (where multi-threaded HTTP servers handle 1,500 RPS across a small fleet of vCPUs without per-request `$0.20/1M` charges, at the cost of managing ALB + container scaling).
expectations: Activates the serverless-architecture-and-cost-advisor skill and calculates the Standard Lambda On-Demand monthly cost (breaking down both `$0.20/1M` request charges and `arm64` GB-second duration charges for 3.94B requests)

Explains how Lambda Managed Instances (LMI) improves TCO for steady I/O-heavy workloads via multi-concurrency (`PerExecutionEnvironmentMaxConcurrency` / `AWS_LAMBDA_MAX_CONCURRENCY`) and EC2 Savings Plans, while highlighting its 15–20 min capacity-provider scale-out and thread-safety / `/tmp` constraints
Contrasts ECS Fargate (plus ALB) TCO and operational trade-offs against Standard Lambda and LMI

evals.prompt: Our order ingestion pipeline runs 200 RPS (518.4 million workflows/month). Each workflow executes 6 steps, finishes in 1.2 seconds total, and consumes 256 MB memory. An engineer built this as an AWS Step Functions Standard Workflow and our projected AWS bill is over $77,000/month! Show the exact state-transition math explaining why Standard Workflows cost $77k+/month here, and calculate the cost and architectural trade-offs of switching to Step Functions Express Workflows vs Lambda Durable Functions.
evals.expected_output: Activates the serverless-architecture-and-cost-advisor skill, calculates the Step Functions Standard Workflow cost (`518.4M workflows * ~6–7 state transitions = ~3.11B–3.63B transitions * $25 / 1M = $77,760–$90,720/month`), contrasts **Step Functions Express Workflows** (max 5-minute duration, billed at `$1.00 / 1M requests` = `$518.40` + duration memory-seconds, cutting orchestration cost by >98% while offering native AWS SDK integrations), and compares **Lambda Durable Functions** (code-first Python/TypeScript `ctx.step` checkpointing without per-state-transition `$25/1M` fees).
expectations: Activates the serverless-architecture-and-cost-advisor skill and shows the exact Step Functions Standard Workflow math (`518.4M executions * 6+ transitions * $25/1M transitions = ~$77,760+/month`)
Calculates the savings of switching to Step Functions Express Workflows (`$1.00/1M executions` + duration, valid because execution time is 1.2s < 5-minute Express limit)
Compares Lambda Durable Functions (`ctx.step` replay model) against Step Functions Express across cost, execution model, and direct AWS SDK integrations

evals.prompt: We are building an AI coding assistant where enterprise customers execute untrusted LLM-generated Python scripts that need persistent in-memory state across interactive turns, strict hardware isolation per session (`sessionId`), up to 16 concurrent tool calls inside the same sandbox, and outbound internet access. Why does standard AWS Lambda fail this requirement, and how should we architect this using Lambda MicroVMs?
evals.expected_output: Activates the serverless-architecture-and-cost-advisor skill, explains that standard Lambda shares warm execution environments across sequential invocations of the same function (making untrusted multi-tenant code unsafe) and limits concurrency to 1 request per environment, and recommends **Lambda MicroVMs** (`Runtime: microvm`, dedicated hardware-isolated MicroVM per `microvmId`, persistent memory/disk across snapshot `/resume`, up to 64 concurrent requests per MicroVM on `:8080`, mandatory CSPRNG `/dev/urandom` reseeding and credential refresh inside `/resume`, and `VpcConfig` Lambda Network Connectors required for outbound internet access).
expectations: Activates the serverless-architecture-and-cost-advisor skill and explains why standard Lambda is unsuitable (shared warm environments across tenants and 1 concurrent request per environment)
Recommends Lambda MicroVMs (`Runtime: microvm`, dedicated hardware isolation per `microvmId`, up to 64 concurrent requests per MicroVM on `:8080`, and stateful snapshot/restore)

Highlights both mandatory MicroVM operational requirements: reseeding CSPRNG (`/dev/urandom`) + refreshing credentials in `/resume`, and attaching `VpcConfig` (Lambda Network Connectors) because MicroVMs have no outbound internet by default

evals.prompt: Our serverless bill in ap-south-1 has three runaway line items that cost more than Lambda itself: (1) $4,500/month in CloudWatch Logs ingestion (9 TB/month of verbose JSON logs across 40 functions with Never Expire retention), (2) $290/month in NAT Gateway charges even though our VPC Lambdas only talk to S3 and DynamoDB, and (3) $1,200/month in AWS WAF Bot Control inspecting static `.js`/`.png` assets and `/health` checks. Provide the FinOps remediation plan and monthly savings math for all three.
evals.expected_output: Activates the serverless-architecture-and-cost-advisor skill and addresses all three hidden cost traps: (1) CloudWatch Logs (`$0.50/GB` on `STANDARD` vs `$0.25/GB` on `INFREQUENT_ACCESS`, setting explicit `RetentionInDays` like 14–30 days, sampling `DEBUG` logs at 1–5%, and using Embedded Metric Format EMF), (2) replacing the NAT Gateways (`~$32.40/mo/AZ` + `$0.045/GB`) with **free VPC Gateway Endpoints** for S3 and DynamoDB (or removing Lambda from the VPC if no private resources exist), and (3) ordering cheap IP/Geo/Rate WAF rules at lower priority numbers first and adding a `ScopeDownStatement` on AWS Managed Bot Control (`$1.00/1M` requests) so it only inspects `/login`, `/signup`, or `/checkout`.
expectations: Activates the serverless-architecture-and-cost-advisor skill and details CloudWatch Logs FinOps optimization (`STANDARD` at `$0.50/GB` vs `INFREQUENT_ACCESS` at `$0.25/GB`, explicit `RetentionInDays`, 1–5% `DEBUG` log sampling, and Embedded Metric Format EMF)
Recommends replacing the NAT Gateways (`~$32.40/mo/AZ` + `$0.045/GB`) with free S3 and DynamoDB VPC Gateway Endpoints (or detaching Lambda from the VPC)

Recommends ordering cheap WAF rules (IP Reputation, Geo, Rate-Based) at lower priority numbers before AWS Managed Bot Control and adding a `ScopeDownStatement` to exclude static assets and health checks

evals.prompt: We are designing three new serverless microservices in ap-south-1: Service A is a shopping cart key-value store needing <5ms p99 latency at 20,000 RPS; Service B is a multi-region active-active double-entry accounting ledger needing strict ACID SQL joins and zero connection pool management; Service C is a geospatial & RAG search service needing PostgreSQL `PostGIS` and `pgvector` HNSW indexes. Using the Persistence Selection Matrix, match each service to the right serverless database and explain the connection/concurrency model for each.
evals.expected_output: Activates the serverless-architecture-and-cost-advisor skill and routes: (1) Service A -> **Amazon DynamoDB** (single-digit ms latency over HTTPS API, zero connection pools, On-Demand scaling), (2) Service B -> **Amazon Aurora DSQL** (serverless active-active distributed SQL with `99.999%` multi-region SLA, IAM token auth, Optimistic Concurrency Control `SQLSTATE 40001` retries, and no connection-pool exhaustion), and (3) Service C -> **Aurora Serverless v2 paired with RDS Data API or RDS Proxy** (because Aurora DSQL does not support `pgvector` or `PostGIS`, and RDS Data API / RDS Proxy prevents Lambda bursts from exhausting PostgreSQL connections).
expectations: Activates the serverless-architecture-and-cost-advisor skill and routes Service A (shopping cart) to Amazon DynamoDB
Routes Service B (multi-region active-active ACID SQL ledger) to Amazon Aurora DSQL, noting its IAM token auth and Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC)
Routes Service C (`PostGIS` + `pgvector`) to Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 paired with RDS Data API or RDS Proxy, explicitly noting that Aurora DSQL does not support PostgreSQL extensions

evals.prompt: I'm new to serverless and writing a Python loan-approval workflow where my code calls a credit bureau API, waits up to 72 hours for a human underwriter to click 'Approve' in an email link, and then disburses the funds. Can I just call `time.sleep(259200)` inside a standard Lambda function, or what are the right AWS serverless options so I don't pay for 72 hours of idle waiting?
evals.expected_output: Activates the serverless-architecture-and-cost-advisor skill, explains that standard Lambda functions have a hard **15-minute execution limit** and bill for every millisecond of active execution (making `time.sleep()` impossible and an anti-pattern), and compares the two zero-idle-compute alternatives: (1) **Lambda Durable Functions** (code-first Python/TypeScript using `ctx.step` and `ctx.wait_for_callback` up to 1 year with **$0 compute cost** while suspended) and (2) **AWS Step Functions Standard Workflows** (up to 1 year using `.waitForTaskToken` callbacks, billed per state transition at `$25 / 1M`).
expectations: Activates the serverless-architecture-and-cost-advisor skill and explains that standard Lambda functions cap at 15 minutes and bill for active wall-clock duration, so `time.sleep()` cannot be used
Recommends Lambda Durable Functions (`ctx.step` + `ctx.wait_for_callback`, up to 1 year duration with $0 compute charge while suspended; noting non-deterministic code must stay inside `ctx.step`)
Compares AWS Step Functions Standard Workflows (`.waitForTaskToken` up to 1 year, billed per state transition at `$0.025 per 1,000` / `$25 per 1M` transitions)
